doc.title: James Hunter interviewed by Monk Rowe, Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Lyrics printed on Daptone records
summary: Hunter explains why Daptone records lacked lyric sheets and how he came round to including them.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Any questions I haven’t asked you that you’d like to comment.
Na. I can’t ask myself questions.
How come there’s no words on the Daptones?

I don’t know. I think it’s just not their policy. I actually fought it when we first did it. I thought we don’t need that. Because I always thought the words aren’t that important enough. And then when they insisted, my manager insisted on my early records, I went along with it and thought no, I don’t mind showing off the lyrics.
Well as Monk said, but at least you can understand the words. You know?

I thought that was my rationale for not including them because they were fairly apparent you know and I think that a lot of records where they did that was because when the backing track would overpower the vocals anyway so you needed subtitles.

Yeah. But I didn’t initially think it was necessary. Now I sort of like it. But I think maybe it’s cause at that time the main thing is the, what do you call it, the vinyl. Vinyl is the main product for them and the CDs are a kind of incidental market for them, and you didn’t tend to get lyrics in with the LPs whereas you get a booklet with the — you tend to get a booklet with the CD. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
The cardboard ones are bad. Although the “Minute by Minute” one has it.
That one did, didn’t it, right up until “Hold On” didn’t have them. Did “Minute by Minute” have the lyrics in?
Yeah it had a slide in.
Yeah that’s right. It did, yeah. I don’t know, I’ll ask them. I won’t to fight tooth and nail because maybe people have more fun figuring them out you know.
Okay. The old fashioned way, you’d sit and write them down.
